{{Short description|Study of strategic interactions on networks}}
{{Multiple issues|
{{Orphan|date=December 2025}}
{{Notability|date=December 2025}}

'''Game theory on networks''' is a field that studies strategy in competing interest interactions among rational or adaptive players that are affected by the topology of networks.<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/> Players' interactions are modeled by a [[network theory|network]] (a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] with nodes for each player, plus additional data). This contains concepts from [[game theory]], [[nonlinear dynamics]], and [[graph theory]] to analyze behavioral player-player phenomena like cooperation, and collective behavior as well as competition and percolation in networked systems.<ref name="nowak1992evolutionary"/><ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>

This field has applications in areas such as [[economics]], [[computer science]], [[biology]], and [[engineering]], where players (nodes) interact through network connections (edges) instead of fully homogeneously mixed populations.<ref name="jackson2008social"/>

== Overview ==
Typical models in game theory assume that all players interact with every other player in a ''well-mixed population'' that is homogeneous.<ref name="hofbauer1998evolutionary"/> However, in ''networked game theory,'' nodes are limited to interact only through edges to other neighboring nodes.<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/> In these networks, each node denotes a unique player while each edge denotes a path through which interactions are possible. These can be represented by payoff matrices that quantify utilities of different competing strategies.<ref name="perc2010coevolutionary"/>

Furthermore, topological features (e.g. degree distribution, clustering, modularity, centrality) in networks can be studied in game theory settings, which may change the evolution, stability, and equilibria of strategies and therefore players.<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>

== Mathematical formulation ==
Consider a graph (or ''network'') <math>G = (V, E)</math> with <math>N = |V|</math> nodes and with an adjacency matrix <math>A = [A_{ij}]</math>.<ref name="jackson2008social"/>
Each node <math>i \in V</math> denotes a unique player with a strategy <math>s_i</math> chosen from a set of strategies <math>S_i</math>.
The payoff for node <math>i</math> is:<ref name="hofbauer1998evolutionary"/>

<math>
u_i(s_i, \mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{N}_i}) = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} A_{ij} P(s_i, s_j)
</math>

where <math>P(s_i, s_j)</math> is some payoff function pairwise between node <math>i</math> each of its neighbors, <math>\mathcal{N}_i</math>.<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/>

A Nash equilibrium of a network is a collection of strategies for each player <math>\mathbf{s}^* = (s_1^*, \dots, s_N^*)</math> such that<ref name="hofbauer1998evolutionary"/>
<math>
u_i(s_i^*, s_{-i}^*) \ge u_i(s_i, s_{-i}^*) \quad \forall i, s_i \in S_i.
</math>

== Evolutionary dynamics ==
In evolutionary networked game theory, each node's strategy changes over time based on its payoff relative to its neighbors.<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/>
Let <math>x_i(t)</math> be the probability that node <math>i</math> uses strategy <math>s_i</math>.
The replicator dynamics in this network are:<ref name="hofbauer1998evolutionary"/>

<math>
\dot{x}_i = x_i(1 - x_i) [\Pi_i^{s_1} - \Pi_i^{s_2}],
</math>

<math>
\Pi_i^{s_1} = \sum_j A_{ij} P(s_1, s_j), \quad
\Pi_i^{s_2} = \sum_j A_{ij} P(s_2, s_j).
</math>

These dynamics are the networked population version of the classical replicator equation for well-mixed populations.<ref name="nowak1992evolutionary"/>

<math>
\dot{x} = x(1 - x) [\Pi_{s_1} - \Pi_{s_2}],
</math>

One often-used structure updating mechanism is the Fermi rule:<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/>

<math>
\Pr(i \leftarrow j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\Pi_j - \Pi_i)/K}},
</math>

where <math>K</math> controls the level of randomness in the imitation process, which is reminiscent of the [[Boltzmann distribution]].<ref name="perc2010coevolutionary"/> In this way, we can compare game theory dynamics to [[statistical mechanics]] models.<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>

== Spectral and topological effects ==
The [[graph Laplacian]], <math>L = D - A</math> (where <math>D</math> is the degree matrix), can be used to determine specific characteristics of the node dynamics.<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>
Linearizing the networked replicator dynamics around an equilibrium yields:<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/>
<math>
\dot{\mathbf{x}} = -L W \mathbf{x},
</math>

where <math>W</math> logs the payoff gradients for local neighbors.
The eigenvalues of <math>L</math> (especially the algebraic connectivity <math>\lambda_2(L)</math>) can be used to calculate rates of convergence and the equilibrium stability.<ref name="jackson2008social"/>
Networks with a modular structure may exhibit slow strategy transition or extremely stable cooperative clusters, which is similar to phenomena observed in spin systems and synchronization.<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>

== Network formation games ==
For network formation games, players can decide to form or delete links in order to strategically maximize utility.<ref name="jackson2008social"/>
If creating a link creates a cost <math>c</math> and yields benefit <math>b_{ij}</math>, a player's payoff can be written as:<ref name="jackson2008social"/>

<math>
u_i(G) = \sum_j b_{ij} - c k_i,
</math>

where <math>k_i</math> is the node's degree.
A network <math>G^*</math> is pairwise stable if:<ref name="jackson2008social"/>

<math>
u_i(G^*) \ge u_i(G^* - ij) \quad \text{and} \quad
u_i(G^* + ij) < u_i(G^*) \text{ or } u_j(G^* + ij) < u_j(G^*).
</math>

Models like these can explain the natural formation of social, economic, and communication networks as being the equilibrium outcomes of decentralized optimization.<ref name="jackson2008social"/>

== Applications ==
Game theory in network science has applications in many fields.<ref name="perc2010coevolutionary"/>

* economics - modeling competition and cooperation in trade networks<ref name="jackson2008social"/>
* biology - modeling evolution of inter- or intra-species cooperation, and host–parasite interactions<ref name="nowak1992evolutionary"/>
* computer science - distributed algorithms, routing, and cybersecurity<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>
* sociology - opinion dynamics, cultural evolution, and collective behavior<ref name="perc2010coevolutionary"/>
* engineering - resource allocation in energy networks<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>

There are many current areas of research <ref name="perc2010coevolutionary"/> that include the following. Multi-layer and temporal networks are games played on multiplex topologies.<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/> Quantum game theory, which is the application of quantum information to strategic interactions on networks.<ref name="szabo2007evolutionary"/> Learning and reinforcement dynamics which covers machine learning in evolutionary games.<ref name="perc2010coevolutionary"/> Control and optimization, which means designing network structures to create desired equilibria<ref name="jackson2008social"/>

Theoretical challenges include extending equilibrium concepts to non-stationary networks and developing scalable analytical approximations.<ref name="hofbauer1998evolutionary"/> In nonlinear dynamics, it is also a large question of how to link microscopic dynamics to macroscopic observables.<ref name="barrat2008dynamical"/>
